Loughbrown Stakes 2026: Preview, Betting Tips + How to Watch

b

betHQ Editor

October 31, 2026

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:53
Instaread

The QuinnBet Loughbrown Stakes (Group 3) is off at 14:37 on Sunday 1 November at the Curragh, over two miles and seventy-one yards, worth €70,000. Eleven run for Pattern company on ground called soft by one source and yielding to soft by another — a stamina test, and one that leaves us with two we cannot separate.

Who’s Fancied — and Why

Amelia Earhart is favourite at 3/1, a three-year-old filly trained by A P O’Brien and ridden by G M Ryan. She tops the eleven on Racing Post Ratings — the form book’s measure of how well a horse has run — and is the quickest of them on Topspeed.

Asakir is next at 10/3, trained by J P Murtagh. The betting likes him more than we do: he is eleven pounds off the best Racing Post Rating here.

Chally Chute at 7/2 has the history: Ross O’Sullivan’s eight-year-old gelding won this race last year under D W O’Connor, who rides him again, and across the thirteen runnings we could check he is the only former winner in the field. He also has the best official rating of the eleven, the handicapper’s figure rather than the form book’s.

The Ground, and Who Has Handled It

The going is the story and it is not settled. On Saturday evening irishracing called the Curragh soft and the Racing Post’s racecard yielding to soft, while At The Races and the Racing Post’s dated index split the track — soft on the straight course, yielding to soft on the round. No source we reached says which course a two-mile race uses, so we will not pretend to know which applies.

Two miles on ground like that is a stamina test before anything else, and one set of figures speaks to it better than the ratings. At The Races publish a record for every runner under a heading their FormScan pages label similar going — runs, wins and places. Chally Chute has run nineteen times on it and won six, more than any of the other ten can show. Amelia Earhart has one win from six.

Our Read

We think the favourite is the likeliest winner and will not dress that up as something cleverer. What we will not tell you is that she is the best horse in the race. Our reading of the form makes Chally Chute the best horse in this field — and Amelia Earhart every bit as good. The two are level on our reading and we cannot separate them. The betting can — she is 3/1, he is 7/2. He is the bigger price and we do not make her the better horse. Our quarrel with the market is his price, not the favourite.

Amelia Earhart tops this field on Racing Post Ratings, is the fastest of the eleven on the clock, and as a three-year-old filly gets nine pounds from Chally Chute. Against that, she has won neither at the Curragh nor over this trip, and one win from six on similar going is thin cover for two miles of it. The ratings say how good she has been; the going record asks whether that carries to Sunday.

The case against the alternative is recent. Seven days ago at Saint-Cloud, over nearly two miles on soft ground, these two met: she finished fourth, he finished sixth, and hers was the better run. Against that afternoon stands a career — the best official rating here, six wins on this kind of ground, and this race itself last year. You have to decide which you trust.

How to Bet This Race

Eleven runners and no handicap, which fixes the terms: all three firms we track print three places at a fifth of the odds. That fifth decides the second bet.

The Likeliest Winner is Amelia Earhart at 3/1, as a win single. Confidence Fair, because our reading does not put her at the head of this field, and because she was out of the places last time and has won over neither this course nor this trip. A £10 win single at 3/1 returns £40, a profit of £30; beaten, the £10 has gone. That assumes the 3/1, there with some firms and a shade shorter at others.

William Hill’s Daily Racing Winnings Boost adds to the return on a winning racing bet, with the qualifying stake capped at £20. It makes nothing more likely to win.

The Alternative is Chally Chute at 7/2, a win single as well. Confidence Strong, because our reading does put him at the head of this field and nothing else here has more wins on ground like this — though he was out of the places seven days ago, with the favourite in front of him. The labels differ by more than the horses do: with nothing between them on our read, one has to come first, and that is convention, not a verdict. A £10 win single at 7/2 returns £45, a profit of £35.

The each-way is a trap here. A £10 each-way bet costs £20 — £10 to win, £10 for the place. Win and it returns £62, a profit of £42, where the same £20 on the win single returns £90 and a profit of £70. Place without winning and it returns £17 on a £20 outlay: three pounds less than you staked. Out of the first three and the £20 has gone. At a fifth of the odds, anything shorter than 5/1 loses money when it only places.

Position Payout suits anyone weighing that up: bet365 pay out by finishing position and show the return for each on their racecard, so you can check the sums yourself.

The Verdict

Amelia Earhart at 3/1 is The Likeliest Winner and takes a win single, confidence Fair because our reading does not put her at the head of this field — the risk being one win from six on similar going.

Chally Chute at 7/2 is The Alternative, also a win single, confidence Strong because our reading puts him at the head of this field and no rival has more wins on similar going — the risk being that the favourite beat him seven days ago.

We will not claim an order we do not have: on our reading the two are level, and only the price divides them. Both bets are win-only on purpose — at 7/2 a placed run hands back £17 on a £20 outlay, less than you staked.

How we pick our tips

Every preview on betHQ starts from the betting market, not against it. The price a horse is trading at is the single best guide anyone has to its chance — it reflects the form book, the money and the opinion of people who do this for a living. So our first question is not “who wins?” but “does our own reading of the form agree with the market, and where doesn’t it?”

We rate every runner on five things: its Racing Post Rating, its Topspeed figure, its Official Rating, how it has run in its last three starts, and how it has fared against the other horses in this race when they have met. We then compare that order with the betting order. Handicaps work differently, because in those the official handicapper sets each horse’s weight from its official rating — so there we adjust the ratings for the weight carried on the day and leave the official rating out, rather than counting the same thing twice.

Most of the time we agree with the market about the likeliest winner, and we say so — across British and Irish racing the favourite wins roughly a third of all races. How often varies a great deal by the type of race, though. Favourites win appreciably more often in conditions races, where horses run off set weights, than in handicaps, where the handicapper’s whole job is to give every runner the same chance; and in the biggest fields their strike rate falls away sharply. That is our first tip. Where we differ is usually further down the betting, and if a horse looks better to us than its price suggests, and is good enough on ratings to be a realistic winner, it becomes our second tip. Some races only get one tip. That is fine.

We also tell you how we would back each one, because the bet you place matters as much as the horse you pick. A short-priced favourite and a 12/1 outsider call for different approaches, and the right bookmaker offer can improve either.

Two things to be clear about. The weightings above are our judgement, not a proven formula — we do not claim to beat the market over time, and nobody should treat our tips as a way to make money. And the prices we quote are the ones showing when we write, the evening before racing; they move, sometimes a lot, so always check the live table before you back anything. Please bet responsibly.
